checkpoints: A userId read straight off a query string with no signature or session check is not authentication — it is a bare, enumerable value, so incrementing it to another user's id and hitting the same endpoint silently unsubscribes a stranger.

A trustworthy unsubscribe link is a server-signed, stateless token carrying userId, channel, category, and an expiry, computed with something like crypto.createHmac and verified using crypto.timingSafeEqual — never `===`, which leaks a byte of timing information per comparison — so the link needs no login yet cannot be forged or replayed past its exp.

A single boolean column on the user entity cannot represent per-channel, per-category consent — it forces "disable marketing SMS" and "disable transactional email" to be the same on/off bit instead of independent choices.

The fix for that granularity problem is a UserPreference row per (userId, channel, category) with a composite unique constraint, written through an idempotent upsert on those three columns, so flipping one preference touches exactly that pair and leaves every sibling channel/category untouched.

Marketing messages rest on consent and must be opt-outable, while OTPs and order confirmations rest on performance-of-contract obligations — gating both kinds of mail behind the same unsubscribed flag risks silently suppressing a login code because of an unrelated marketing opt-out click.

Because transactional messages are not consent-based, an unsubscribe endpoint should explicitly refuse to act on a transactional category — returning 400 Bad Request — rather than honoring the opt-out as if it applied.

Stamping deletedAt on the User row while the id and every UserPreference row remain intact is still personal-data processing, so it does not satisfy GDPR Article 17 erasure; genuine erasure means deleting the user row and all associated preference rows in one transaction, keeping at most a one-way-hashed audit entry as proof erasure occurred.

A still-valid unsubscribe token clicked after the underlying user has already been erased is an idempotent edge case: the endpoint should return 200 with nothing left to update rather than throw a 500 on a missing row.
